title: Task Scheduler
description: Schedule tasks with a cooldown between same-type executions, using a max-heap plus cooldown queue simulation reduced to a closed-form frequency formula.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a character array tasks and a non-negative integer n, a CPU processes one task per unit of time, but the same task type must be separated by at least n intervals (idle time allowed). Return the minimum number of time units needed to complete all tasks.

blocks.caption: A max-heap picks the most-needed ready task each tick; a cooldown queue tracks when each task type becomes ready again.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","tasks[] (characters A-Z), n (cooldown between same-type executions)"],["Rule","The same task type cannot run again until at least n other time units have passed"],["Idle allowed","If no task is ready, the CPU can sit idle for one unit"],["Output","Minimum total time units to finish every task"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

A cooldown before an item becomes usable again is a strong signal for a queue holding (item, time it becomes ready), paired with a way to pick the highest-priority ready item, which is what a max-heap provides. This "heap for priority, queue for cooldown" combination is a recurring scheduling pattern.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The most frequent task should always be scheduled first whenever it is ready, since it has the most remaining copies to fit into the schedule and the least slack.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a chef who can cook the same dish again only after it has cooled down for n minutes. Each minute, the chef should cook whichever ready dish is needed most (has the most remaining orders), to keep the kitchen as busy as possible. If nothing is ready, the chef must wait a minute idle.

blocks.caption: The busiest dish is prioritized whenever it is off cooldown.

items: Only the FREQUENCY of each task type matters, not which specific task it is.
The most frequent task type dictates the schedule's overall shape, since it needs the most gaps of size n between its own executions.
If there are enough OTHER distinct task types to fill every gap left by the most frequent task, no idle time is needed at all.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
tasks = [A,A,A,B,B,B], n = 2. Both A and B occur 3 times, the maximum frequency.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: A must be separated by at least 2 slots from itself, creating 2 gaps of size 3 (A _ _ A _ _ A), for a "frame" of (3-1)*(2+1) = 6 slots before the last A, plus 1 for the last A itself = 7 slots, and B fits into every one of the 2 idle gaps alongside A, but since B ALSO has frequency 3, both A and B need their own final slot, giving countMax = 2, so the total is 6 + 2 = 8, matching the visible schedule above.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct simulation greedily picks the most-frequent ready task each time unit, using a max-heap for "which task is most needed right now" and a queue for "which tasks are currently cooling down and when do they become ready again." This is correct and intuitive but processes one time unit at a time.

The key mathematical insight: only the task type(s) with the MAXIMUM frequency determine the schedule's minimum length. Picture placing the most frequent task first, creating (maxFreq - 1) gaps of size n after each of its occurrences except the last, i.e. a "frame" of (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) slots. Any OTHER task type, including additional types tied for maxFreq, fills into these gaps; only if there are more total tasks than the frame can hold does the total length become simply the total task count instead (everything packs tightly with no idle time at all).
6. Brute Force Solution

Simulate time unit by unit: a max-heap holds remaining counts of ready task types, and a queue holds task types currently on cooldown along with the time they become ready again. Each tick, run the top of the heap if available (decrementing its count and queuing it for cooldown if any remain), then move any task whose cooldown just expired back into the heap.

codes.python:
import heapq
from collections import Counter, deque


def least_interval(tasks, n):
    freq = Counter(tasks)
    heap = [-c for c in freq.values()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    cooldown = deque()
    time = 0

    while heap or cooldown:
        time += 1
        if heap:
            count = -heapq.heappop(heap) - 1
            if count > 0:
                cooldown.append((count, time + n))
        if cooldown and cooldown[0][1] == time:
            count, _ = cooldown.popleft()
            heapq.heappush(heap, -count)

    return time


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(least_interval(["A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"], 2))
    print(least_interval(["A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"], 0))

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(total_time * log 26)","One heap operation per time unit, and total_time can include idle slots"],["Space","O(26)","At most 26 distinct task types in the heap and cooldown queue combined"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Simulating every single time unit, including idle ones, is unnecessary work once it is recognized that the answer follows directly from just the frequency counts.
8. Optimize the Solution

Skip the simulation entirely. Count each task type's frequency, find the maximum frequency, and count how many task types share that maximum. The answer is the larger of two values: the "frame" size (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countMax, or simply the total number of tasks (which wins whenever there are enough distinct task types to pack the schedule with zero idle time).

items: Count frequencies of all 26 possible task types, O(len(tasks)).
Find maxFreq and countMax by scanning the 26 frequency buckets, O(26), effectively O(1).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A cooldown-before-reuse constraint is naturally modeled with a max-heap for priority plus a queue for tracking when items become ready again.
When only counts (not identities or order) matter, look for a closed-form formula instead of simulating every step.
The "frame built around the most frequent item" idea generalizes to any scheduling problem where one dominant item dictates the minimum achievable spacing.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Task Scheduler is solved by recognizing that the task type(s) with maximum frequency determine a minimum "frame" size around which every other task fits. Comparing this frame size against the raw total task count gives the answer directly in O(len(tasks)) time, replacing a tick-by-tick heap simulation with a simple frequency-counting formula.
